sec:
Vote by mail or absentee

Can’t get to your polling place on Election Day? Here is how to vote by mail in Minnesota, from the state’s own election office and its laws. Checked October 21, 2026.

Ask for your ballot by

Monday, November 2Passed

The law lets you apply up to one day before the election: Monday, November 2, 2026. The Secretary of State suggests applying at least two weeks ahead online (by Tuesday, October 20) so there is time for the ballot to travel both ways by mail; that suggested date has passed, so if you apply now, think about returning the ballot in person or voting early in person. (the law)

Send it back by

Tuesday, November 3Passed

A ballot sent by mail must reach your election office by 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026; a postmark is not enough. A ballot you or someone you choose hands in at the election office must arrive by 5 p.m. on Election Day. (the law)

The last day to ask for a ballot by mail has passed. You can still vote in person, early or on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3.You can still vote in person on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3. Early voting in person runs through Monday, November 2, 2026. When and where to vote early.

Ask for a ballot online, on Minnesota’s own site

At school away from home, in Minnesota or in another state? What Minnesota says about students is under Show more.

Who can vote by mail

No reason is needed. State law says any eligible voter may vote by absentee ballot. You do not have to be registered before you apply. (the law)

How to ask for a ballot

  • Online. Apply on the Secretary of State's website. You need an email address and your Minnesota driver's license or ID card number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number. Open it (official page)
  • By mail. Download a paper application and send it to your county election office by mail, email or fax. Open it (official page)
  • In person. You can hand in a written application in person at your county auditor's office, or your city or town clerk's office if it handles absentee ballots. (the law)

How to send it back

  • By mail. Mail it in the return envelope that comes with your ballot. It must arrive by 8 p.m. on Election Day. (the law)
  • Drop box. Your county or city may set up official drop boxes for absentee ballots. (the law)
  • In person. Hand it in at the county auditor's or city clerk's office that sent it, by 5 p.m. on Election Day. You may also name a person (an agent) to hand it in or mail it for you; one agent can do this for no more than three voters in an election. (the law)

What the envelope needs

A witness must watch you mark your ballot. The witness can be any U.S. citizen who will be 18 by Election Day, or a notary, and must see your blank ballot before you vote. On the signature envelope you write the same kind of ID number you gave when you applied: your Minnesota driver's license or ID card number, or the last four digits of your Social Security number (or mark that you have none). (the law)

Track your ballot

Track your ballot on Minnesota’s own site (official page)

Vote early in person instead

Friday, September 18, 2026 to Monday, November 2, 2026.

You can vote early in person at your county election office (and any other place your county names) during the 46 days before the election, from Friday, September 18 through Monday, November 2, 2026. During the last 18 days (from Friday, October 16), early voting is also offered at the county auditor's office and any other polling place the auditor names. (the law)

Students

At school in Minnesota, away from home

We could not read the Secretary of State's own page for students (its site answered our request with a check for human visitors). The state's residence law says your home is where you live and usually sleep and intend to return to; you do not lose your home address by living somewhere else for a while, and you do not gain a new one by staying somewhere only for a while. The absentee application asks for both your home address and the address where the ballot should be mailed, so a student registered at home can have the ballot sent to school. (the law)

At school in another state, with Minnesota as home

State law says you do not lose your Minnesota residence by living for a while in another state, but you do lose it if you move to another state meaning to live there for an indefinite time. The absentee application asks for a mailing address apart from your home address, so a student who keeps Minnesota as home can have a Minnesota absentee ballot mailed out of state. (the law)

Military and overseas

Members of the military, their spouses and dependents, and citizens outside the United States can vote absentee the regular way or through the federal process, using the Federal Post Card Application to register and ask for a ballot (by mail, email or fax). For November 3, 2026, Minnesota sets no earlier deadline to register or ask: both may be received as late as Election Day. The voted ballot must be returned by mail and received by 8 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, so allow for mail time. (federal guide)

Minnesota in the Federal Voting Assistance Program’s guide

Good to know

  • Some small Minnesota towns and townships hold their elections entirely by mail; we did not read that rule's source, so it is not described here.
  • The Federal Voting Assistance Program's state guide was read through the content feed its own page loads.

How this was checked

  • The Secretary of State's site answered our second request with a check for human visitors, so only its main vote-by-mail page was read; deadlines and rules here come from that page and from state law. Your county election office can confirm local details such as drop box places and hours.

Checked October 21, 2026. Rules and dates can change: Minnesota’s election office, and your county or local election office, have the final word.

polls:
Polls are open 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. (some small towns open later). (the law)

Anyone in line when the polls close may still vote.
